Forbidden
for-bid'n
v. and a. (prohibited by authority; of what the commandments forbid, and of the door the Holy Ghost shut against Paul in Asia)
From Old English forbeodan, to command against, from the prefix for-, expressing prohibition, and beodan, to bid. The Greek at Acts 16:6 is koluo, to hinder or prevent — the same verb used when our Lord forbids the disciples to hinder the children.

Biblical Definition

Two uses of the word run through Scripture, and they must be kept apart. The first is moral prohibition. “And if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the LORD; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity” (Leviticus 5:17). The clause though he wist it not is the striking one: ignorance of the prohibition does not dissolve the guilt, though the law provides a sacrifice for it — a standing rebuke to the notion that sin requires conscious intent. Moses applies the same to the second commandment: “make you a graven image, or the likeness of any thing, which the LORD thy God hath forbidden thee” (Deuteronomy 4:23). The second use is providential rather than moral: “Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” (Acts 16:6), followed by “they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not” (Acts 16:7). Nothing sinful was proposed; preaching the word in Asia was a good thing, and Paul would later do it at length. The closed door was not a rebuke but a redirection, and it ended at Troas with the vision of the man of Macedonia.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines forbid as to prohibit, to interdict, to command not to do a thing, and also to oppose or hinder.

FORBIDDEN, pp. Prohibited; interdicted; hindered; obstructed.

FORBID, v.t. To prohibit; to interdict; to command to forbear or not to do.

The laws of God forbid us to swear.

2. To command not to enter; to hinder; to restrain.

3. To oppose; to obstruct; to render impracticable.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 5:17 — "And if a soul sin, and commit any of these things which are forbidden to be done by the commandments of the LORD; though he wist it not, yet is he guilty, and shall bear his iniquity."

Deuteronomy 4:23 — "Take heed unto yourselves, lest ye forget the covenant of the LORD your God, which he made with you, and make you a graven image, or the likeness of any thing, which the LORD thy God hath forbidden thee."

Acts 16:6 — "Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia,"

Acts 16:7 — "After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not."

Modern Corruption

Sin is redefined as requiring conscious intent, so that Leviticus 5:17 becomes unintelligible and much of the law becomes optional.

expand to see more

The prevailing moral instinct is that a man is culpable only for what he meant. Leviticus 5:17 states the opposite plainly: he commits a forbidden thing, he wist it not, he is guilty, and he shall bear his iniquity. The Reformed doctrine of sins of ignorance follows from this text and from Psalm 19:12, who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults. The point is not to make God arbitrary; it is that God's law defines sin, and a creature's awareness does not create or dissolve the standard. The gospel implication is enormous, since no man knows the full extent of his own guilt, and therefore no man can measure the atonement he needs. The law which convicts a man of what he did not know he did is the law that drives him to a Substitute.

The second use has its own live corruption, in the opposite direction. Acts 16 is regularly read as a template for reading providence as personal direction, so that any closed door becomes the Spirit's specific instruction and any open one a divine endorsement. Luke does not encourage the method. He records an apostolic band being hindered twice and then given an explicit vision, and he offers no technique for distinguishing the Spirit's restraint from ordinary difficulty. Paul, hindered from Asia, did not stop; he kept moving until the way opened. Obedience proceeds by the revealed will of God in Scripture, with providence read afterwards, not as a substitute for it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mitsvah, commandment — Leviticus 5:17; tsavah, to command — Deuteronomy 4:23; Greek koluo, to hinder or forbid — Acts 16:6.

expand to see more

Hebrew mitsvah — commandment; Leviticus 5:17, “the commandments of the LORD.”

Hebrew tsavah — to lay charge upon, command; Deuteronomy 4:23 of the graven image.

Greek koluo — to hinder, forbid, prevent; Acts 16:6, and Mark 10:14 of the children.

Greek eao — to permit, suffer; Acts 16:7, “the Spirit suffered them not.”

Old English forbeodan, to command against — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“Though he wist it not, yet is he guilty” — sins of ignorance are still sins."

"“Forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” — a good thing, shut for a season."

"“The Spirit suffered them not” — the second closed door, and then Troas."
